abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions—task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning–execution–verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.

sections.body: The section argues that open-world robot autonomy requires evaluating the whole loop of task discovery, reasoning, execution and recovery, which existing benchmarks do not measure together. It introduces RobotAgentBench, built with an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline into 50 household layouts. The benchmark contains 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks and 4 open-ended scenarios. Task-level evaluation covers five dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery and disturbance handling. Scenario-level evaluation tests how these capabilities combine. The authors report five findings, including that standalone policies struggle with discovery and reasoning, that recursive self-improvement (RSI) progressively improves performance, and that real-world runs show degradation but broadly consistent rankings.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Current benchmarks test isolated manipulation skills, so this work proposes a benchmark for full robot autonomy in household settings.

sections.body: The section describes how the benchmark is constructed and scored. A physical room in a real home is reconstructed in Isaac Sim, with a coding agent retrieving and adjusting similar 3D assets and human reviewers checking visual fidelity and physical consistency. The room is expanded into 50 layouts by changing floor plans, furniture positions and appearance. Teleoperated demonstrations on the AgiBot G1 robot are replayed in simulation and extended with coding-agent trajectories. The suite has 90 atomic tasks, composed into 18 short-horizon and 8 long-horizon tasks, with 50 training trajectories per atomic and short-horizon task and 101.8 hours of training data in total. Four scenario metrics are defined: Task Coverage, Task Progress, Recovery Rate and Stagnation.
sections.heading: RobotAgentBench
sections.headline: Real rooms are rebuilt in simulation to create 50 layouts, and five agent architectures are compared under one framework.

sections.body: The section reports task-level and scenario-level experiments comparing standalone VLA and WAM baselines with five agent designs. Codex is the coding agent throughout, with InternVLA-A1.5 as the learned policy where applicable, and each task or scenario is evaluated on 30 instances. In Table 1, the highest standalone Average is 18.0 for InternVLA-A1.5. The hybrid design C/H/C scores 48.5 on Average and 15.4 on Open-Ended. The fully code-based Codex design scores 31.0 and 8.4, and its recursive self-improvement variant reaches 42.3 and 10.8 in the final of ten iterations. On matched evaluation subsets, simulation and real-world results differ; Codex averages 34.2 in simulation and 31.9 in the real world.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Standalone policies average at most 18.0, while the best agent, a hybrid code and learned-policy design, reaches 48.5.
